summary: Defines how audio in the PureVoice format is packed into RTP packets for sending over IP networks.

eli5.summary: A speech-squashing format needs a standard way to fit its sound into network packets, and this says how.

questions: what is the rtp payload format for purevoice
how many codec frames can one rtp packet hold
subtitle: How to pack Qualcomm PureVoice (Qcelp) speech frames into RTP packets, with optional interleaving to hide packet loss.

tldr.problem: The PureVoice (Qcelp) speech codec produces small frames of different sizes, and a lost network packet can wipe out a run of consecutive frames, which sounds bad.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP payload starts with one octet carrying interleave settings, followed by one or more codec data frames. The sender can bundle several frames per packet and spread neighbouring frames across different packets (interleaving), so a lost packet leaves scattered gaps instead of one big hole.
tldr.outcome: Receivers must support interleaving and feed erasure frames to the codec for anything missing, which lets the codec interpolate over short gaps. Senders choose how much delay to trade for loss tolerance.

today: RFC 2658 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1999, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction and the Qcelp Codec
sections.content:
RFC 2658 describes how compressed audio from the Qualcomm PureVoice codec (also called Qcelp, defined in the EIA/TIA standard IS-733) is carried as an RTP payload type. It also provides an interleaving method so that lost packets degrade quality less. The sender can pick an interleave setting depending on whether low end-to-end delay or greater tolerance for lost packets matters more.

The RFC notes that IS-733 is the standard codec for CDMA wireless terminals and that the codec is also used in several Internet applications. Every 20 milliseconds of 8000 Hz, 16-bit sampled speech is compressed into one of four frame sizes: Rate 1 (266 bits), Rate 1/2 (124 bits), Rate 1/4 (54 bits) or Rate 1/8 (20 bits). The codec picks the rate by analysing the speech and its operating mode (normal or reduced rate). For typical speech this averages 6.8 k bits/sec in normal mode and 4.7 k bits/sec in reduced rate mode.
sections.eli5: The codec squashes every little slice of speech into a tiny package. Quiet moments get very small packages and busy sounds get bigger ones.

sections.title: The RTP Payload Header
sections.content:
The RTP timestamp uses units of 1/8000 of a second. The payload begins with a single octet holding three fields, followed by one or more codec data frames that are aligned on octet boundaries. The RTP header has its expected values, the extension bit is not set, and this payload type never sets the marker bit. When several frames or interleaving are in use, the timestamp is that of the oldest data in the packet.

  • RR (2 bits): reserved. The sender MUST set it to zero and the receiver SHOULD ignore it.
  • LLL (3 bits): the interleave value. It MUST be between 0 and 5 inclusive; 6 and 7 MUST NOT be used by senders. A non-zero value means interleaving is enabled.
  • NNN (3 bits): the interleave index, which MUST be less than or equal to LLL.

All receivers MUST support interleaving. Senders MAY support it, and a sender that does not MUST set both LLL and NNN to zero. A packet with an invalid LLL or NNN is treated by the receiver as lost.
sections.eli5: The first byte of every packet is a small label that says how the cards are being shuffled and which card this one is.

sections.title: Codec Data Frame Format
sections.content:
Each codec data frame starts with an octet 0 that gives the rate and the total frame size. Value 0 is a Blank frame of 1 octet, 1 is Rate 1/8 (4 octets), 2 is Rate 1/4 (8 octets), 3 is Rate 1/2 (17 octets) and 4 is Rate 1 (35 octets). Value 5 is reserved (8 octets) and 14 is an Erasure frame (1 octet) that senders SHOULD NOT transmit. Any other value is reserved, and a frame with a reserved value in octet 0 is treated as invalid data.

After octet 0, the bits of the codec's own frame are packed from the highest numbered bit to the lowest, starting at the most significant bit of octet 1. Unused bits in the last octet MUST be set to zero. For example, a Rate 1/8 frame has octet 0 equal to 1, then bits 19 down to 0, then four zero bits, for 4 octets in total.
sections.eli5: Each little package has a size tag on the front, then the sound bits packed tightly, with any leftover space filled with zeros.

sections.title: Bundling and Interleaving
sections.content:
A sender MAY bundle several codec data frames into one RTP packet. There is no count field, so a receiver finds the frames by reading octet 0 of each one in turn until the packet ends. Receivers MUST handle bundles of up to 10 frames. Senders MUST NOT bundle more than 10 frames or more than fit in the MTU, and for that calculation every frame is assumed to be Rate 1 size.

Interleaving only matters when more than one frame is bundled. With bundling value B and interleave value L, a group of B * (L+1) consecutive frames is spread over L+1 packets. Packet 0 (NNN=0) carries frames 0, L+1, 2(L+1) and so on; packet 1 carries frames 1, 1+L+1 and so on; the last carries frames starting at L. Packets in a group MUST be sent in increasing NNN order and in increasing timestamp order.

Once a sender starts with a given SSRC, it MUST NOT increase the bundling value or the interleave value; to raise either it MUST use a new SSRC. It MAY decrease them, but only between interleave groups, and never raise them again afterwards. This lets a receiver size its buffer once and never need more.

A receiver finds the group boundaries from the sequence number S and index N: the group is the packets numbered S-N through S-N+L. The expected bundling value is that of the first packet of the group that arrives. If a packet has a different count, the receiver MAY trim frames, pad with erasure frames, or discard the whole group and play silence.
sections.eli5: Instead of putting neighbouring words on the same card, the sender deals them out like a deck of cards to several envelopes. The receiver collects the envelopes and puts the words back in order.

sections.title: Handling Lost Packets
sections.content:
The Qcelp codec understands erasure frames, which stand for frames that are not available. Receivers MUST feed erasure frames to the codec for all missing data, and the codec interpolates the missing audio. Receivers MUST use the timestamp clock to count missing frames, because each codec data frame advances the timestamp by exactly 160 counts and the bundling value may change. A missing packet in an interleave group counts as B erasure frames.

If a late packet arrives before its next frame is needed, receivers SHOULD use it instead of an erasure frame. The RFC explains that listeners perceive the best quality when erasure frames are not consecutive, which is why interleaving helps, but interleaving can greatly increase end-to-end delay. For interactive sessions it recommends an LLL of 0 or 1 with a bundling factor of 4 or less. When delay does not matter, it recommends a bundling value of at least 4 and an LLL of 4 or 5, subject to MTU limits.
sections.eli5: If a card is lost, the listener's decoder makes an educated guess for the missing bit. Guessing works much better when only single words are missing, not a whole phrase.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Packets in this format are subject to the security considerations of the RTP specification and any appropriate profile. Confidentiality is achieved by encryption, and since compression is applied end to end, encryption can be done after compression without conflict.

The RFC says a denial-of-service attack is possible against codecs whose decoding effort varies a lot, because an attacker could inject packets that are expensive to decode, but this encoding does not show any significant non-uniformity. As with any IP protocol, a receiver can also be overloaded simply by too many packets.
sections.eli5: Locks on the mail are handled by the normal RTP rules. This codec does not give attackers an easy way to make the listener's decoder work extra hard.

fields.name: RR
fields.desc: Reserved; sender sets zero, receiver ignores.

fields.name: LLL
fields.desc: Interleave value, 0 to 5; non-zero enables interleaving.

fields.name: NNN
fields.desc: Interleave index, at most the value of LLL.

data.title: Interleave group of 4 frames in 2 packets
data.code:
Frames from the codec, in time order: 0 1 2 3

Packet 1: LLL=1 NNN=0  carries frames 0, 2
Packet 2: LLL=1 NNN=1  carries frames 1, 3

If packet 2 is lost, frames 1 and 3 are erased,
not two frames in a row.
